opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think held-out internal benchmarks are one of the most important tools we have. Public benchmarks are useful for comparing against the rest of the field, but once a benchmark has been out in the world for a while, it starts to leak. Pieces of it end up on the web, people discuss the answers, and it becomes hard to know whether a model is actually getting better at the underlying skill or has just seen something close to the test set during training. So having evaluations that we keep internal, that have never been published and aren't anywhere on the web, gives us a much cleaner signal.

The way we use them is mostly as a guide to where the model is weak. You want benchmarks in a regime where the model isn't already saturating them. If you're at 95 or 98 percent, there's not much more you can learn; the remaining errors might just be label noise. The most useful ones are where the model is at maybe 10, 20, 30 percent, because that tells you there's a real capability gap. Then you can ask what we'd need to change to improve that: more or better training data in some area, a change to the training recipe, a different way of using inference-time compute, or an architectural change.

They also act as a check on ourselves. When you're making lots of changes to a training setup, you want to know that an improvement on one thing isn't quietly regressing something else. A broad suite of held-out evals across coding, math, long-context reasoning, multilingual capabilities and so on lets you see the whole picture rather than optimizing for one number.

And you have to keep refreshing them. As models get more capable, you need harder evaluations, and you want them to reflect what people actually want to use these models for, not just what's easy to measure. That's part of the craft: building evaluations that track the capabilities you care about, and keeping them clean enough that you can trust what they're telling you.

r001.rationale: The response says low benchmark performance reveals a capability gap, then asks what to change, including more or better training data in that area or an architectural change.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something we think about a lot, because the public benchmarks have this problem where the moment they become well known, they start leaking into training data, or people start optimizing for them specifically, and then they stop telling you very much. A benchmark is only useful as long as it's actually measuring the thing you care about rather than measuring how well you've memorized the benchmark.

So internally we try to maintain a set of evaluations that are held out in a pretty strict sense. The team that builds them is somewhat separated from the teams doing the model training, the data is not in any training corpus we can see, and we're careful about how often we look at results, because even if the data isn't in the training set, if you iterate against a number thirty times a day you're going to overfit to it through the humans in the loop. That's a subtle kind of contamination that people underestimate.

The other thing I'd say is that we try to make these evals look like real tasks rather than multiple choice questions. Things like, can the model take a reasonably messy codebase and make a change that actually passes the tests, or can it work through a long document and answer questions that require synthesizing across many parts of it, or can it do some multi-step reasoning where getting the intermediate steps right actually matters. Those are harder to game, and they correlate better with whether users find the model useful.

And then how you use them to guide improvements is really about diagnosis. When we see a gap, we want to understand whether it's a data problem, an architecture problem, a scale problem, or something about how we're doing post-training. So we'll often have a suite that's sliced pretty finely, so you can say, okay, the model got better at long context retrieval but worse at this particular kind of math, and that points you toward a specific thing to go investigate. A single aggregate number doesn't really help you decide what to do next. Having lots of fine-grained signals, kept clean, is what makes it actionable.

And then periodically you have to retire them and build new ones, because eventually the model just gets good at them and they saturate, and that's fine, that's actually the goal.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark gaps are used for diagnosis, including whether they reflect a data problem or an architecture problem, to guide what to investigate next.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to separate the signal you use to guide development from the signal you use to check whether you’ve actually made progress. If you repeatedly look at a held-out benchmark and make changes based on it, it gradually becomes part of your development process, even if you never train on those examples directly.

So you want a set of evaluations that helps you understand weaknesses—is the model struggling with reasoning, following instructions, or using information in a long context? Those can guide experiments with data, training, and the model itself. Then you want a separate, fresh set of problems to check whether the improvements generalize.

And I’d look beyond the aggregate score. Two models can get the same score and have very different failure modes. Looking at what they get wrong helps you formulate a hypothesis, run an experiment, and see whether you improved the underlying capability.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark-identified weaknesses can guide experiments with data, training, and the model, but does not clearly specify task-specific training data or model architecture as the choices.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic idea is to keep some evaluations separate from the data you’re using to train the model, so you can ask: is this change actually helping it generalize? You want a range of tasks, because a single aggregate score can hide a lot. A model might get better at coding while becoming less reliable at following instructions.

Then you look at the failures. Is the model missing some knowledge? Is it struggling with a multistep problem? Does it understand the task but produce an answer in the wrong format? Those suggest different things to improve, whether that’s the training data, the training process, or the model itself.

There’s a subtlety, though: if you keep making decisions based on the same held-out benchmark, you’re effectively tuning to it. So you need fresh evaluations and a separate check that the improvements carry over to tasks people actually care about.

r001.rationale: It says benchmark failure patterns suggest what to improve, including the training data or the model itself, which communicates using identified capability gaps to guide those improvement decisions.
